claim: Spindle orientation is often achieved by a complex of Partner of Inscuteable (Pins)/LGN, Mushroom Body Defect (Mud)/Nuclear Mitotic Apparatus (NuMa), Gαi, and Dynein, which interacts with astral microtubules to rotate the spindle.
source: Spindle orientation is often achieved by a complex of Partner of Inscuteable (Pins)/LGN, Mushroom Body Defect (Mud)/Nuclear Mitotic Apparatus (NuMa), Gαi, and Dynein, which interacts with astral microtubules to rotate the spindle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this mechanism.

claim: Cortical Pins/LGN recruitment serves as a critical step in spindle orientation.
source: Cortical Pins/LGN recruitment serves as a critical step in this process.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about the role of Pins/LGN in spindle orientation.

claim: Pins-mediated planar cell polarized divisions occur in several mitotic domains of the early Drosophila embryo.
source: Here, we identify Pins-mediated planar cell polarized divisions in several of the mitotic domains of the early Drosophila embryo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and data presented in the manuscript showing Pins polarization in mitotic domains.

claim: Neither planar cell polarity pathways nor planar polarized myosin localization determined division orientation in the mitotic domains studied.
source: We found that neither planar cell polarity pathways nor planar polarized myosin localization determined division orientation
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that disruption of these pathways did not affect division orientation.

claim: Pins planar polarity and force generated from mesoderm invagination are important for division orientation.
source: instead, our findings strongly suggest that Pins planar polarity and force generated from mesoderm invagination are important.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple perturbations including laser ablation and Snail depletion.

claim: Disrupting Pins polarity via overexpression of a myristoylated version of Pins caused randomized division angles.
source: Disrupting Pins polarity via overexpression of a myristoylated version of Pins caused randomized division angles.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing randomized division angles in myr-Pins expressing embryos.

claim: Disrupting forces through chemical inhibitors, depletion of an adherens junction protein, or blocking mesoderm invagination disrupted Pins planar polarity and spindle orientation.
source: We found that disrupting forces through chemical inhibitors, depletion of an adherens junction protein, or blocking mesoderm invagination disrupted Pins planar polarity and spindle orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CytoD injections, α-catenin RNAi, and Snail depletion experiments.

claim: Directional ablations that separated mesoderm from mitotic domains disrupted spindle orientation.
source: Furthermore, directional ablations that separated mesoderm from mitotic domains disrupted spindle orientation
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments showing disrupted spindle orientation after AP cuts.

claim: Forces transmitted from mesoderm to mitotic domains can polarize Pins and orient division during gastrulation.
source: suggesting that forces transmitted from mesoderm to mitotic domains can polarize Pins and orient division during gastrulation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of laser ablation, Snail depletion, and Pins localization experiments.

claim: This is the first in vivo example where mechanical force has been shown to polarize Pins to mediate division orientation.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first in vivo example where mechanical force has been shown to polarize Pins to mediate division orientation.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature and their experimental findings.

claim: Epithelial morphogenesis and homeostasis are influenced by cell division orientation.
source: Epithelial morphogenesis and homeostasis are influenced by cell division orientation, which can occur along specific axes relative to both the epithelial plane and the polarity of an organ/organism (Baena-López et al., 2005; Kulukian and Fuchs, 2013; Lancaster and Knoblich, 2012; Morin and Bellaïche, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Epithelia are tissues composed of cells that are organized in a sheet and held together by junctions.
source: Epithelia are tissues composed of cells that are organized in a sheet and held together by junctions, which maintain the integrity of the tissue as well as the apical-basal polarity of cells (Choi et al., 2013; Classen et al., 2005; Cox et al., 1996; Gumbiner, 2005; Harris and Peifer, 2005; Tepass, 1997; Wang and Margolis, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing the structure of epithelia.

claim: Spindle orientation determines division orientation.
source: Orientation of the mitotic spindle is what determines whether a division is symmetric or not, as spindle orientation determines division orientation (Cabernard and Doe, 2009; Gönczy and Rose, 2005; Lechler and Fuchs, 2005; Mao et al., 2011; Nakajima et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In Drosophila neuroblasts, asymmetric division and spindle orientation is dependent on Pins/LGN recruitment to the apical cortex.
source: In Drosophila neuroblasts, asymmetric division and spindle orientation is dependent on Pins/LGN recruitment to the apical cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about neuroblast division.

claim: Apical proteins recruit Inscuteable (Insc), which in turn recruits Pins/LGN and the spindle rotation complex.
source: Apical proteins recruit Inscuteable (Insc), which in turn recruits Pins/LGN and the spindle rotation complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about the molecular pathway in neuroblasts.

claim: Pins null mutants exhibit defects in spindle orientation in neuroblasts.
source: Pins null mutants exhibit defects in spindle orientation in neuroblasts (Cabernard and Doe, 2009; Schaefer et al., 2000; Siller et al., 2006; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In symmetric epithelial cell divisions, spindle orientation depends on Pins, which is recruited to the lateral cortex by the lateral domain protein, Discs large (Dlg).
source: In symmetric epithelial cell divisions, spindle orientation also depends on Pins, which is recruited to the lateral cortex by the lateral domain protein, Discs large (Dlg).
evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about epithelial cell division.

claim: Loss of Pins, Dlg, or disrupted recruitment of Pins by Dlg causes aberrant asymmetric cell divisions in epithelia and cell loss.
source: Loss of Pins, Dlg, or disrupted recruitment of Pins by Dlg causes aberrant asymmetric cell divisions in epithelia and cell loss (Bell et al., 2015; Bergstralh et al., 2013; Carvalho et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In planar cell polarized divisions of the sensory organ precursor (SOP) cells in the Drosophila dorsal thorax, asymmetric determinant segregation and spindle orientation depend on planar polarized Pins and E-cadherin localization, respectively.
source: Furthermore, in planar cell polarized divisions of the sensory organ precursor (SOP) cells in the Drosophila dorsal thorax, asymmetric determinant segregation and spindle orientation depend on planar polarized Pins and E-cadherin localization, respectively (Bellaïche et al., 2001; Le Borgne et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In isolated cell cultures, cell division orientation has been shown to directly respond to stress by aligning with applied forces.
source: For example, in isolated cell cultures, cell division orientation has been shown to directly respond to stress by aligning with applied forces (Fink et al., 2011; Matsumura et al., 2016; Théry et al., 2007; Théry et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The connection between cell shape and division axis is known as the long axis rule or Hertwig's rule and was first observed over 100 years ago.
source: The connection between cell shape and division axis is known as the long axis rule or Hertwig's rule and was first observed over 100 years ago (Hertwig, 1884).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to historical literature.

claim: In epithelial tissues, cell division/spindle orientation occurs along the tension axis, which can dissipate tension and influence cell packing.
source: In epithelial tissues, cell division/spindle orientation occurs along the tension axis, which can dissipate tension and influence cell packing (Campinho et al., 2013; Gibson et al., 2011; Godard et al., 2020; Mao et al., 2011; Scarpa et al., 2018; Wyatt et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the Drosophila pupal notum and Xenopus, cell shape has been shown to affect the spindle angle through the influence of molecular cues localized at tricellular junctions.
source: In the Drosophila pupal notum and Xenopus, cell shape has been shown to affect the spindle angle through the influence of molecular cues localized at tricellular junctions, which provide a 'memory' for interphase cell shape (Bosveld et al., 2016; Nestor-Bergmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the Drosophila oocyte, follicular epithelium, and parasegmental boundaries and cultured MDCK cells, molecular cues, like Pins/LGN and Mud/NUMA, do not localize to tricellular junctions.
source: In contrast, in the Drosophila oocyte, follicular epithelium, and parasegmental boundaries and cultured MDCK cells, molecular cues, like Pins/LGN and Mud/NUMA, do not localize to tricellular junctions, implying that cells use additional strategies to promote force-oriented spindle rotation, in some contexts (Finegan et al., 2019; Gloerich et al., 2017; Scarpa et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mechanical cues have been shown to recruit the Pins/LGN machinery to adherens junctions in MDCK cells.
source: For example, mechanical cues have been shown to recruit the Pins/LGN machinery to adherens junctions in MDCK cells (Hart et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mitotic rounding forces have been shown to be important for proper spindle orientation and morphology.
source: Mitotic rounding forces have also been shown to be important for proper spindle orientation and morphology (Chanet et al., 2017; Kunda et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: During development, the early Drosophila embryo undergoes 13 cycles of synchronous nuclear divisions with no intervening gap phases.
source: During development, the early Drosophila embryo undergoes 13 cycles of synchronous nuclear divisions with no intervening gap phases.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: After 13 cycles of nuclear division, embryonic cells arrest in G2.
source: After these 13 cycles of nuclear division, embryonic cells arrest in G2.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Cycle 14 divisions occur in a highly stereotyped pattern defined by string (Drosophila Cdc25 homologue) expression in pockets of cells across the embryo.
source: Cycle 14 divisions occur in a highly stereotyped pattern defined by string (Drosophila Cdc25 homologue) expression in pockets of cells across the embryo.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila development.

claim: Pockets of cells that divide together are termed mitotic domains.
source: These pockets of cells that divide together are termed mitotic domains (Edgar and O'Farrell, 1989; Foe, 1989).
evidence: This claim is based on established terminology supported by citations.

claim: Some mitotic domains have been observed to have oriented divisions, but the mechanism underlying division orientation is unknown.
source: Some of these domains have been observed to have oriented divisions, but the mechanism underlying division orientation is unknown (da Silva and Vincent, 2007; Hartenstein and Campos-Ortega, 1985; Hartenstein et al., 1987; Stern et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and sets up the research question.

claim: Spindle orientation is a dynamic process in which spindles are not assembled in position, but rather rotate to achieve orientation in mitotic domains 1, 3, and 5.
source: We found that spindle orientation is a dynamic process in which spindles are not assembled in position, but rather rotate to achieve orientation in mitotic domains 1, 3, and 5 (MDs 1, 3, and 5) in the dorsal 'head'
evidence: This claim is supported by live imaging data showing spindle rotation.

claim: Spindles in MDs 1, 3, and 5 are oriented in the direction of eventual tissue movement/elongation.
source: and are oriented in the direction of eventual tissue movement/elongation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the orientation data and knowledge of tissue movements.

claim: Oriented symmetric divisions in MDs 1, 3, and 5 and MD14 require planar polarized Pins.
source: We discovered that these oriented symmetric divisions and those of MD14, which had previously been shown to exhibit force-dependent oriented symmetric divisions (Wang et al., 2017), require planar polarized Pins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Pins polarization and the effects of disrupting it.

claim: MD3 is the anterior most mitotic domain and comprises around 30 cells.
source: MD3 is the anterior most mitotic domain and comprises around 30 cells
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation and counting of cells in the manuscript.

claim: MD1 is the next most anterior domain and consists of two mirrored clusters of around 40 cells.
source: MD1 is the next most anterior domain and consists of two mirrored clusters of around 40 cells
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation and counting of cells in the manuscript.

claim: MD5 is located just anterior to the cephalic furrow and consists of two mirrored clusters containing around 30 cells.
source: and MD5 is located just anterior to the cephalic furrow and consists of two mirrored clusters containing around 30 cells (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation and counting of cells in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: MD1 cells exhibit planar polarized cell division.
source: MD1 cells exhibit planar polarized cell division.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing oriented cytokinetic rings.

claim: Cytokinetic rings in MDs 1, 3, and 5 are oriented roughly perpendicular to the anterior-posterior (AP) axis.
source: In MDs 1, 3, and 5, cytokinetic rings are oriented roughly perpendicular to the anterior-posterior (AP) axis (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 1C.

claim: Mitotic spindles in MDs 1, 3, and 5 are not initially oriented with the AP axis and form with no preferential orientation.
source: Notably, we found that mitotic spindles are not initially oriented with the AP axis and form with no preferential orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing initial random spindle orientation.

claim: Spindles in MDs 1, 3, and 5 rotated up to 90° to achieve a final orientation.
source: Spindles then rotated up to 90° to achieve a final orientation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data in Figure 1D.

claim: There is no chirality in spindle rotation in MD1.
source: Despite dividing with a mirror-symmetric tilt away from the AP axis, we observed no chirality in spindle rotation; on the left side of MD1 53% of measured spindles rotated counterclockwise and 47% rotated clockwise, on the right side 46% rotated counterclockwise and 54% clockwise.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of spindle rotation direction.

claim: MDs 1, 3, and 5 exhibited oriented divisions achieved by spindle rotation toward an angle ~30° from the AP axis.
source: Together these data show that MDs 1, 3, and 5 exhibited oriented divisions and this orientation is achieved by spindle rotation toward an angle ~30° from the AP axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of division angles shown in rose plots.

claim: MDs 1, 3, and 5 all exhibit planar cell polarity of Pins.
source: We discovered that MDs 1, 3, and 5 all exhibit planar cell polarity of Pins.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing polarized Pins localization.

claim: The Pins planar cell polarity is dependent on cell cycle state: mitotic cells exhibit planar polarized Pins, whereas Pins is uniformly distributed along lateral membranes of interphase cells.
source: The Pins planar cell polarity is dependent on cell cycle state: mitotic cells exhibit planar polarized Pins, whereas Pins is uniformly distributed along lateral membranes of interphase cells (Figure 2A, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing Pins localization changes during cell cycle.

claim: In MD1, the Pins intensity is highest on the posterior side of the cells and the crescent of Pins intensity peaks just past the posterior-most point of the cell cortex.
source: We found that in MD1, the Pins intensity is highest on the posterior side of the cells and the crescent of Pins intensity peaks just past the posterior-most point of the cell cortex (Figure 2C and C').
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative intensity measurements shown in Figure 2C and C'.

claim: The ratio of the point of greatest Pins intensity to the average of the two adjacent troughs averaged over three embryos was significantly greater than the same ratio calculated from the Gap43::mCherry signal.
source: The ratio of the point of greatest Pins intensity to the average of the two adjacent troughs averaged over three embryos was significantly greater than the same ratio calculated from the Gap43::mCherry signal (peak-to-trough ratio Pins, 1.39±0.1017 and Gap43::mCherry, 1.04±0.0406, mean and SD, p=1.7057e-08)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative statistical analysis of intensity measurements.

claim: Pins polarity is not caused by membrane inhomogeneity.
source: demonstrating that this polarity was not caused by membrane inhomogeneity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of Pins and Gap43 intensity ratios.

claim: Pins was enriched on the posterior side of MDs 1 and 3, but the anterior side of MD5.
source: Interestingly, from observation of boundary cells, we find Pins was enriched on the posterior side of MDs 1 and 3, but the anterior side of MD5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenous Pins was planar polarized in mitotic MD1 cells.
source: We found that similar to Pins::YFP, endogenous Pins was planar polarized in mitotic MD1 cells (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data in fixed embryos shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: Mud follows a similar localization pattern as Pins and is polarized in crescents in mitotic cells of MD1.
source: It appears that Mud follows a similar localization pattern as Pins and is polarized in crescents in mitotic cells of MD1, although Mud also strongly labels spindle poles (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Mitotic cells within MD14 exhibited planar polarized Pins.
source: Mitotic cells within MD14 exhibited planar polarized Pins, similar to what we saw for MD1 (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The peak-to-trough ratio for Pins in MD14 was significantly different from control Gap43::mCherry.
source: The peak-to-trough ratio for Pins in MD14 was significantly different from control Gap43::mCherry (1.22±0.0914 and 1.04±0.1115, respectively, mean and SD, p=3.1726e-06) (Figure 2H–K').
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative statistical analysis shown in Figure 2H-K'.

claim: Pins polarization preceded spindle rotation.
source: We found that Pins polarization preceded spindle rotation and is abolished shortly after anaphase, when the spindle position is finalized (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: There is a strong correlation between angular position of maximum Pins intensity and the anaphase spindle angle in MD1.
source: We found that there was a strong correlation between angular position of maximum Pins intensity and the anaphase spindle angle in MD1 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3C with R²=0.77.

claim: Division orientation correlates with Pins localization, but not interphase cell shape.
source: Together these data show that division orientation correlates with Pins localization, but not interphase cell shape.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation analyses comparing Pins angle vs division angle and cell shape vs division angle.

claim: Overexpression of myristoylated Pins caused Pins to be uniformly distributed along the membrane during mitosis and abolished Pins planar polarity.
source: Overexpression of myristoylated Pins, but not wild-type Pins, caused Pins to be uniformly distributed along the membrane during mitosis and abolished Pins planar polarity (Figure 2C', Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 2C' and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Perturbation using myr-Pins did not obviously disrupt other morphogenetic events during gastrulation.
source: Importantly, perturbation using myr-Pins did not obviously disrupt other morphogenetic events during gastrulation. Mesoderm invagination, cephalic furrow invagination, and germ band extension all occur in embryos expressing myr-Pins.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of embryos expressing myr-Pins.

claim: Expression of myr-Pins does not impact the number, timing, or position of cells dividing within the mitotic domains.
source: Further, expression of myr-Pins does not impact the number, timing, or position of cells dividing within the mitotic domains.
evidence: This claim is based on observation and analysis of myr-Pins expressing embryos.

claim: Spindles in embryos expressing myristoylated Pins fail to orient along the AP axis.
source: Despite occurring in-plane, spindles in embryos expressing myristoylated Pins fail to orient along the AP axis. Instead, division angles are evenly distributed, occurring with seemingly no preference between the DV and AP axes for cells within MD1 (Figure 3I–J, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of division angles shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: Myr-Pins expressing embryos had an average division angle within MD1 that was significantly different from controls.
source: Myr-Pins expressing embryos had an average division angle within MD1 that was significantly different from controls (42.7 and 20.1, respectively, p=0.000103).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of division angles.

claim: Myristoylated Pins expression disrupted division orientation in MD14.
source: Myristoylated Pins expression also disrupted division orientation in MD14. Myr-Pins expressing embryos had an average division angle within MD14 that was significantly different from controls (41.2 and 18.1, respectively, p=0.0079) (Figure 3K–N).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3K-N.

claim: Pins polarity is necessary for mitotic spindle orientation and planar polarity of divisions within MDs 1, 3, 5, and 14.
source: These data suggest that Pins polarity is necessary for mitotic spindle orientation and planar polarity of divisions within MDs 1, 3, 5, and 14.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the myr-Pins perturbation experiments showing disrupted orientation.

claim: The Fat-Dachsous and core PCP pathways are not expressed early enough and/or in the MDs to be involved in division orientation.
source: The Fat-Dachsous and core PCP pathways were not good candidates for orienting divisions within MDs 1, 3, and, 5 because previous work has shown the components of these pathways are not expressed early enough and/or in the MDs to be involved (Clark et al., 1995; Tomancak et al., 2002; Tomancak et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on gene expression patterns.

claim: Bazooka (Baz) did not exhibit planar cell polarity in the MDs.
source: The PAR pathway was also not a good candidate because the Drosophila homologue of Par 3, Bazooka (Baz), did not exhibit planar cell polarity in the MDs, despite retaining apical localization during mitosis (Ko et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Injection of dsRNA of TLRs 2, 6, and 8 did not have a significant impact on division orientation.
source: Injection of dsRNA of TLRs 2, 6, and 8 did not have a significant impact on division orientation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The triple TLR mutant perturbation was significantly different from controls but did not randomize division orientation to the extent of expressing Myr-Pins.
source: The triple TLR mutant perturbation was significantly different from controls but did not randomize division orientation to the extent of expressing Myr-Pins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Myo II and Baz were not planar polarized in the Drosophila head.
source: Finally, Myo II and Baz were not planar polarized in the Drosophila head (Chanet et al., 2017; Ko et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: TLRs are not solely responsible for division orientation in MDs 1, 3, 5.
source: leading us to conclude that TLRs are not solely responsible for division orientation in MDs 1, 3, 5.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the TLR perturbation experiments and observations of Myo II and Baz.

claim: AJs mechanically couple epithelial cells, serve as platforms for protein assembly, and are composed of cadherin-catenin complexes.
source: AJs mechanically couple epithelial cells, serve as platforms for protein assembly, and are composed of cadherin-catenin complexes (Hinck et al., 1994; Kovacs and Yap, 2008; Leckband and Prakasam, 2006; Oda et al., 1994; Rimm et al., 1995; Takeichi, 1991; Yap et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on adherens junctions.

claim: AJs are connected to F-actin, which is required for force transmission.
source: AJs are connected to F-actin, which is required for force transmission (Desai et al., 2013; Rimm et al., 1995; Yonemura et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: E-cadherin is able to recruit Pins in a tension-dependent manner.
source: Previous work has shown that E-cadherin is able to recruit Pins in a tension-dependent manner (Hart et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: αcat depletion is the most severe way to disrupt adherens junctions, totally uncoupling mesoderm cell actomyosin from the junctions, preventing their apical constriction, and lowering adherens junction levels throughout the entire embryo.
source: We have shown that αcat depletion is the most severe way to disrupt adherens junctions, totally uncoupling mesoderm cell actomyosin from the junctions, preventing their apical constriction, and lowering adherens junction levels throughout the entire embryo (Denk-Lobnig et al., 2021; Yevick et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claim: Embryos expressing the αcat RNAi had an even distribution of division angles in MD1.
source: When compared to a control RNAi (Rh3), embryos expressing the αcat RNAi had an even distribution of division angles in MD1, occurring with seemingly no preference between the DV and AP axes.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of division angles in αcat RNAi embryos.

claim: αcat-depleted embryos exhibited an average division angle that was significantly different from controls.
source: αcat-depleted embryos exhibited an average division angle that was significantly different from controls (36.7 and 26.4, respectively; p=0.000583) (Figure 4A–D, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4A-D.

claim: Embryos with greater reductions in adhesion exhibited more severe disruption of division orientation.
source: We found that embryos with greater reductions in adhesion (i.e. more rounded cell morphology) exhibited more severe disruption of division orientation (Figure 4E)
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of individual embryos shown in Figure 4E.

claim: AJs and possibly force transmission are required for spindle orientation.
source: consistent with AJs and possibly force transmission being required for spindle orientation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the αcat RNAi experiments.

claim: Cno depletion does not significantly disrupt division orientation within MDs 1, 3, and 5 compared to controls.
source: Measuring division angles, as previously described, we found that Cno depletion does not significantly disrupt division orientation within MDs 1, 3, and 5 compared to controls, Cno-depleted embryos exhibited an average division angle that was not significantly different from controls (27.9 and 26.4, respectively; p=0.2698) (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: Pins planar polarity is abolished when αcat was depleted.
source: In contrast to control embryos, we found that Pins planar polarity is abolished when αcat was depleted (Figure 5A–D, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: Pins peak-to-trough ratio at the posterior was different in controls compared to αcat-depleted embryos.
source: Pins peak-to-trough ratio at the posterior was different in controls compared to αcat-depleted embryos (1.33±0.0751 and 1.06±0.0173, respectively, mean and SD, p=1.1887e-08).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of intensity measurements.

claim: AJs are involved in Pins planar polarization in MD1.
source: These data demonstrate a role for AJs in Pins planar polarization in MD1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the αcat depletion experiments showing loss of Pins polarity.

claim: Injections of CytoD disrupted planar polarized division orientation.
source: We found that injections of CytoD disrupted planar polarized division orientation, CytoD injected embryos exhibited an average division angle that was significantly different from controls (53.7 and 21.9, respectively; p=0.0043) (Figure 6B, D, F and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 6B, D, F and H.

claim: Pins localization was disrupted in embryos injected with CytoD.
source: In addition, Pins localization was disrupted in embryos injected with CytoD whereas Pins exhibited normal polarity in DMSO injected controls (Figure 6A, C, E and G, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6A, C, E and G.

claim: The posterior Pins peak-to-trough ratio was different for DMSO injected controls and CytoD injected embryos.
source: The posterior Pins peak-to-trough ratio was different for DMSO injected controls and CytoD injected embryos (1.17±0.0685 and 1.08±0.0609, respectively, mean and SD, p=6.5007e-11).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of intensity measurements.

claim: DMSO injection seemed to perturb the synchrony of divisions.
source: Interestingly, DMSO injection seemed to perturb the synchrony of divisions. In non-injected embryos, cells within the domain divide in a wave-like pattern, starting in the middle of the domain and propagating to the domain boundary (Di Talia and Wieschaus, 2012). In DMSO injected embryos, nearly all cells round and divide simultaneously.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of DMSO injected embryos and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Division timing disruption did not disrupt division orientation or Pins polarization.
source: This division timing disruption did not disrupt division orientation or Pins polarization.
evidence: This claim is based on observation and analysis of DMSO injected embryos.

claim: Cells that divide within the mechanically isolated region fail to orient along the AP axis.
source: Cells that divide within the mechanically isolated region fail to orient along the AP axis (Figure 6K and M).
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 6K and M.

claim: In sham ablated control embryos, spindles oriented with preference toward the AP axis and had an average division angle that was significantly different from cells within the cut region.
source: In sham ablated control embryos, spindles oriented with preference toward the AP axis and had an average division angle that was significantly different from cells within the cut region (20.0 and 58.0, respectively; p=0.0286) (Figure 6J-M, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 6J-M.

claim: DV oriented laser ablations in the posterior part of MD5 to separate the dorsal head from the cephalic furrow resulted in cells exhibiting oriented divisions.
source: We made DV oriented (horizontal) laser ablations in the posterior part of MD5 to separate the dorsal head from the cephalic furrow and found that cells exhibited oriented divisions, occurring with an average division angle similar to control sham ablations (18.3 and 20.0, respectively; p=1) (Figure 6N, Figure 6—figure supplement 2C D E, Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 6N.

claim: AP oriented line ablations ventral to the head MDs, which separated them from putative pulling forces from the mesoderm, resulted in a random distribution of division angles.
source: In contrast, we found that AP oriented line ablations ventral to the head MDs, which separated them from putative pulling forces from the mesoderm, resulted in a random distribution of division angles, similar to complete isolation of the MD (40.0 and 20.0, respectively; p=0.0286) (Figure 6O, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A B E, Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by laser ablation experiments shown in Figure 6O.

claim: Snail depletion disrupted division orientation.
source: We found that Snail depletion disrupted division orientation (Figure 7B, D, F and H, Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B, D, F and H.

claim: Embryos injected with Snail dsRNA had a random distribution of division angles, occurring with an average division angle significantly different from controls.
source: Embryos injected with Snail dsRNA had a random distribution of division angles, occurring with an average division angle significantly different from controls (40.0 and 22.6, respectively; p=0.0121).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of Snail depletion experiments.

claim: Pins polarity was disrupted in embryos injected with Snail dsRNA.
source: In addition, Pins polarity was clearly disrupted in embryos injected with Snail dsRNA. For 0.1× TE buffer injected controls, the posterior Pins peak-to-trough ratio was different from Snail dsRNA injected embryos (1.27±0.08401 and to 1.10±0.10545, respectively, mean and SD, p=6.7956e-08) (Figure 7A, C, E and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 7A, C, E and G.

claim: Injections of Snail dsRNA disrupted the patterning of MDs 1, 3, and 5.
source: Beyond division orientation and Pins polarity, injections of Snail dsRNA disrupted the patterning of MDs 1, 3, and 5. Instead of three distinct domains, a single group of anterior cells divide.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of Snail-depleted embryos.

claim: Morphogenetic forces play a role in Pins polarity and division orientation within MDs 1, 3, and 5.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that morphogenetic forces play a role in Pins polarity and division orientation within MDs 1, 3, and 5.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combination of αcat, CytoD, laser ablation, and Snail depletion experiments.

claim: Pins exhibits planar cell polarity in mitotic domains of the dorsal head (MDs 1, 3, and 5) and along the ventral midline (MD14).
source: Here, we discovered that Pins exhibits planar cell polarity in mitotic domains of the dorsal head (MDs 1, 3, and 5) and along the ventral midline (MD14).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing Pins polarization in these domains.

claim: Pins polarity is required for spindle orientation.
source: We demonstrated that Pins polarity is required for spindle orientation by overexpressing a myristoylated version of Pins that exhibits unregulated cortical localization and disrupts spindle orientation.
evidence: This claim is supported by myr-Pins overexpression experiments.

claim: Pins planar cell polarity and AP spindle orientation depend on adherens junctions.
source: We found that Pins planar cell polarity and AP spindle orientation depend on adherens junctions.
evidence: This claim is supported by αcat RNAi experiments showing loss of Pins polarity and spindle orientation.

claim: Force transmission through the tissue orients Pins and cell divisions.
source: This and our finding that actomyosin disruption also prevents Pins planar cell polarity led us to hypothesize that force transmission through the tissue orients Pins and cell divisions.
evidence: This claim is a hypothesis inferred from the αcat and CytoD experiments.

claim: Forces from ventral furrow formation are critical for spindle orientation.
source: We showed that forces from ventral furrow formation were critical for spindle orientation, by (1) mechanically isolating MD1 cells from all surrounding tissue (Figure 7I, purple lines), (2) mechanically isolating MD1 cells specifically from the ventral furrow via directional laser ablations (Figure 7I, red lines), and (3) showing that disrupting ventral furrow formation via Snail depletion abrogates proper spindle orientation and Pins localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental evidence including laser ablation and Snail depletion.

claim: Mud localizes to tricellular junctions in the fly notum.
source: Mud localizes to tricellular junctions which cues spindle orientation (Bosveld et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mud does not localize to tricellular junctions within the dorsal head mitotic domains and along the ventral midline.
source: We did not observe Mud localization to tricellular junctions within the dorsal head mitotic domains and along the ventral midline.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of Mud localization in the manuscript.

claim: There is no correlation between cell long axis and division orientation within the dorsal head mitotic domains.
source: Furthermore, we find no correlation between cell long axis and division orientation within these domains, while we find a strong correlation between Pins polarity and cell division angle.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isotropic myosin-dependent tension is required for cell rounding and for symmetric cell divisions in MD cells.
source: However, isotropic myosin-dependent tension is required for cell rounding and for symmetric cell divisions in MD cells (Chanet et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Anisotropic myosin-dependent tension was not observed in the head MDs.
source: In the head MDs, we did not observe anisotropic myosin-dependent tension. Instead, we observe a uniform distribution of actin and myosin along interfaces of cells.
evidence: This claim is based on observation of myosin localization in the manuscript.

claim: E-cadherin is localized asymmetrically and coordinates the asymmetric divisions within Drosophila male germline stem cells and SOP cells.
source: Notably, within Drosophila male germline stem cells (Inaba et al., 2010) and SOP cells (Le Borgne et al., 2002). The adherens junction component, E-cadherin, is localized asymmetrically and coordinates the asymmetric divisions within these cells
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Perturbation of E-cadherin results in misorientation of the mitotic spindle in germline stem cells and SOP cells.
source: and perturbation of E-cadherin results in misorientation of the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In SOP cells, perturbation of E-cadherin disrupted the Pins localization.
source: Interestingly, in SOP cells it was also shown that perturbation of E-cadherin disrupted the Pins localization, although Pins still appears as a crescent (Le Borgne et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In MDCK cells E-cadherin recruits Pins in a tension-dependent manner.
source: In MDCK cells E-cadherin recruits Pins in a tension-dependent manner (Hart et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Adherens junctions may sense anisotropic force or shear forces within the tissue and recruit spindle rotation machinery in a polarized fashion to cue division orientation.
source: As seen in the MDCK cells, in cells within the dorsal head mitotic domains and ventral midline, adherens junctions may sense anisotropic force or shear forces within the tissue and recruit spindle rotation machinery in a polarized fashion to cue division orientation.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the MDCK cell findings and the authors' data.

claim: Mechanical tension and tissue flow has been shown to orient other planar cell polarity proteins.
source: Mechanical tension and tissue flow has been shown to orient other planar cell polarity proteins (Aigouy et al., 2010; Aw et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Whole-embryo light-sheet imaging has revealed a connection between mesoderm invagination and posterior, mediolateral flows in the head.
source: Whole-embryo light-sheet imaging has revealed a connection between mesoderm invagination and posterior, mediolateral flows in the head (Stern et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The oriented divisions of the ventral midline (MD14) have been shown to alleviate tissue strain and promote tissue elongation by promoting an increase in surface area of the mesectoderm.
source: The oriented divisions of the ventral midline (MD14) have been shown to alleviate tissue strain and promote tissue elongation by promoting an increase in surface area of the mesectoderm (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Oriented division facilitates tissue elongation during development.
source: This agrees with other studies which suggest that oriented division facilitate tissue elongation during development (Aigouy et al., 2010; Baena-López et al., 2005; Gong et al., 2004; Mao et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cell divisions compensate for the cell loss due to various invaginations during gastrulation.
source: A recent study followed all the cell intercalations, movements, and divisions during gastrulation, showing cell divisions compensate for the cell loss due to various invaginations (Stern et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Cell division can lead to oriented pushing forces that could contribute to morphogenesis.
source: Indeed, past work has shown that cell division can lead to oriented pushing forces that could contribute to morphogenesis (Gupta et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Apical relaxation that results from mitotic entry and the following oriented division has been shown to give rise to ectopic tissue folds.
source: In the embryo, apical relaxation that results from mitotic entry and the following oriented division has been shown to give rise to ectopic tissue folds (Ko et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The oriented division of the dorsal head facilitates tissue elongation and compensates for cell loss from mesoderm and endoderm invagination.
source: Therefore, we speculate that the oriented division of the dorsal head facilitates tissue elongation and compensates for cell loss from mesoderm and endoderm invagination.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on inference from the data and prior literature.

claim: Snail depletion most severely depletes apical actomyosin activity, and thus pulling forces, in the ventral furrow.
source: To perturb mesoderm invagination, we disrupted the transcription factor Snail because Snail depletion most severely depletes apical actomyosin activity, and thus pulling forces, in the ventral furrow (Martin et al., 2009; Mason et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Myristoylated Pins is functional and able to rescue off-axis divisions that occur after Dlg-RNAi.
source: We have previously shown myristoylated Pins is functional and able to rescue off-axis divisions that occur after Dlg-RNAi (Chanet et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The Pins null mutant causes aberrant out-of-plane divisions.
source: We overexpressed the myristoylated version of Pins instead of using a Pins null mutant because we and others have previously shown that the Pins null mutant causes aberrant out-of-plane divisions and our goal was to disrupt Pins polarity while keeping the divisions in-plane (Chanet et al., 2017; Izumi et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cno-RNAi disrupted myosin localization, similarly to genetic mutants.
source: Note that Cno-RNAi with these lines disrupted myosin localization, similarly to genetic mutants (Sawyer et al., 2011; Sawyer et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Cno-RNAi did not fully abrogate midline convergence during ventral furrow formation, unlike αcat RNAi.
source: but did not fully abrogate midline convergence during ventral furrow formation (Jodoin et al., 2015), unlike αcat RNAi (Denk-Lobnig et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The divisions of MDs 1, 3, 5, and 14 take place during gastrulation.
source: Given that the divisions of MDs 1, 3, 5, and 14 take place during gastrulation
evidence: This claim is based on the timing of divisions observed in the manuscript.

claim: Ventral furrow formation pulls ectoderm cells around the circumference of the embryo.
source: The divisions in MDs 1, 3, and 5 occur during gastrulation, ventral furrow formation pulls ectoderm cells around the circumference of the embryo (Lye et al., 2015; Rauzi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mean division angle for MD1 is 21.6°.
source: Mean division angle for MD1 = 21.6°, MD3=20.4°, and MD5=19.0°.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in the manuscript.

claim: The mean division angle for MD3 is 20.4°.
source: Mean division angle for MD1 = 21.6°, MD3=20.4°, and MD5=19.0°.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in the manuscript.

claim: The mean division angle for MD5 is 19.0°.
source: Mean division angle for MD1 = 21.6°, MD3=20.4°, and MD5=19.0°.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in the manuscript.
